messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 60
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Warehouse Worker
- Trauma Type: Military
- Pcl5: 62

He is 60 now, a warehouse worker with thick hands and a back that stiffens by the end of each shift, and he tells his story in pieces at first, as if each part has to be tested before it can be set down fully. He grew up in Europe and joined the military young, less from patriotism than from habit and expectation. At the time, he liked structure, the certainty of being told where to stand and what to carry. He says that before the deployment he thought of himself as steady, the kind of man other people relied on.

The event he returns to happened decades ago, but he speaks about it as if it is still arranged in front of him. His unit was traveling in convoy through a rural area. He remembers the heat trapped inside the vehicle, the smell of metal and fuel, the irritated joking between men who had been tired too long. Then there was an explosion so sudden that he says his mind still cannot fit a before and after together. The vehicle ahead of his was hit. He remembers sound disappearing for a moment, then coming back all at once in screams, radio static, and shouted orders. He remembers running toward the smoke because that was what he had been trained to do. One of the men he pulled at was someone he knew well, a friend with whom he had shared cigarettes and complaints and long, dull hours. He can still feel the weight of the man’s gear, the unnatural slackness in his body, the heat on his own face as ammunition cooked off nearby. He says that what stays with him most is not just the sight of the injuries, but the moment he understood there was nothing more he could do.

Afterward he kept functioning. He followed orders, finished the deployment, and did what the others did—drank when there was a chance, laughed too loudly, said very little that mattered. He tells himself then that he is lucky, because he survived. At the same time, he begins carrying a private conviction that he has failed in some essential way. He thinks he should have moved faster, seen something earlier, dragged harder, done more. Back home, people greet him as if he has returned intact. He lets them believe it.

Over the years he builds an ordinary life from the outside. He works practical jobs and eventually settles into warehouse work, where the routine suits him: the loading schedules, the pallets, the inventory gun, the satisfaction of putting objects in the right place. He likes being in motion and keeping his mind on tasks that have clear outcomes. But even there, his body behaves as if danger is always close. If a pallet drops unexpectedly or a forklift backfires, he jerks so violently that coworkers turn to look. He laughs it off, calls himself jumpy, but his heart races for long minutes afterward. He checks exits without meaning to. He dislikes having anyone walk up behind him in the aisles and becomes irritable when younger men horse around near heavy equipment.

Sleep has been bad for years. His partner tells him he thrashes and shouts in a language he rarely uses during the day. Some nights he wakes soaked in sweat, already halfway out of bed, his fists clenched before he knows where he is. On those nights he goes to the kitchen rather than risk lying back down. He sits in the dark with coffee long before dawn, staring at the garden or the street, waiting for his breathing to slow. If he does sleep again, he often wakes with the image of smoke and twisted metal pressing into him so sharply that the whole day feels contaminated.

He avoids more than he first admits. He does not go to military commemorations, though he says he “never cared for ceremony.” He keeps his service photographs in a box in the back of a cupboard. When documentaries or news footage show armored vehicles or explosions, he leaves the room or becomes abruptly angry at the television. His partner has learned not to ask too many questions when his mood shifts this way. He knows this hurts her. She says he is present in practical ways—he fixes things, shops for groceries, pays bills on time—but emotionally he disappears without warning. He can sit silently through an entire evening, unreachable, as if he is listening to something happening far away.

Lately he feels older, and that seems to make the memories less containable rather than less intense. At work, when he is tired, he loses track of simple instructions and then curses himself for it. He feels constantly on guard and just as constantly worn out by being on guard. Crowded supermarkets make him sweat; traffic jams leave him gripping the steering wheel until his hands ache. He trusts very few people. He says the world has never again felt entirely ordinary.

What troubles him most is that the past does not stay in the past. A smell of diesel, a burst of static on a radio, the sight of black smoke from a roadside fire—these can pull him back before he has time to think. In those moments he is no longer a 60-year-old man in work boots and a fluorescent vest. He is a young soldier again, running toward wreckage, certain that someone is dying and that he is already too late.
